dal_bhat_adaptations.title: Dal Bhat Adaptations for Dialysis
dal_bhat_adaptations.content: Use smaller portions of dal (1/4 cup), choose low-potassium vegetables, and rinse rice before cooking. Add safe spices like cumin and coriander.

safe_breakfast_options.title: Safe Traditional Breakfast Options
safe_breakfast_options.content: Chiura (beaten rice) with small amounts of curd, sel roti in moderation, or dhindo made with buckwheat flour are good options.

festival_food_modifications.title: Festival Food Modifications
festival_food_modifications.content: During festivals, choose white meat over red, limit sweets, avoid dried fruits and nuts. Focus on rice-based dishes.

newari_dish_modifications.title: Newari Dish Modifications
newari_dish_modifications.content: Choose steamed momos over fried, limit achar portions, avoid alcohol, and opt for rice-based items like chatamari.

hyperkalemia.title: Hyperkalemia (High Potassium) Management
hyperkalemia.description: Low-potassium foods and cooking techniques to manage elevated potassium levels

k1.title: Low-Potassium Nepali Staples
k1.content: Choose white rice (चामल) over brown rice, refined wheat flour (मैदा) products, and white bread. These refined grains have significantly less potassium than whole grains.

k2.title: Double-Boiling Technique for Vegetables
k2.content: Cut vegetables into small pieces, boil for 3-5 minutes, drain completely, then boil again in fresh water. This removes 30-50% of potassium. Perfect for preparing तरकारी (vegetables).

k3.title: Safe Fruits for High Potassium
k3.content: Choose apples (स्याउ), pears, berries, and grapes. Limit to 1-2 servings daily. Avoid bananas, oranges, and melons completely.

k4.title: Protein Sources Low in Potassium
k4.content: Egg whites, fish, and chicken breast are excellent low-potassium protein sources. Limit red meat and avoid organ meats.

hyperphosphatemia.title: Hyperphosphatemia (High Phosphorus) Management
hyperphosphatemia.description: Low-phosphorus diet strategies and phosphate binder timing

p1.title: Avoiding High-Phosphorus Foods
p1.content: Completely avoid organ meats, nuts, seeds, and dark colas. Limit dairy products including milk, yogurt, and cheese. Choose white bread over whole grain.

p2.title: Phosphate Binder Timing
p2.content: Take phosphate binders with the first bite of every meal and snack containing protein. Never skip binders with dal, meat, or dairy products.

p3.title: Safe Nepali Protein Alternatives
p3.content: Choose egg whites over whole eggs, fish over red meat, and limit dal to 1/4 cup per meal. Soak dal overnight and discard soaking water.

p4.title: Reading Food Labels for Phosphorus
p4.content: Avoid processed foods with phosphorus additives (phosphoric acid, sodium phosphate). Choose fresh foods over packaged ones.

combined.title: Combined Low Potassium + Low Phosphorus Diet
combined.description: Foods and strategies suitable for both potassium and phosphorus restrictions

c1.title: Double-Safe Food Choices
c1.content: Rice, cauliflower (double-boiled), cabbage, apples, and egg whites are safe for both restrictions. These should form the base of your diet.

c2.title: Meal Planning Strategy
c2.content: Plan meals around safe carbs (rice, pasta), double-boiled vegetables, and limited high-quality protein. Take phosphate binders with every meal.

c3.title: Traditional Nepali Adaptations
c3.content: Modify dal-bhat: use 1/4 cup dal (soaked overnight), double-boil vegetables, serve with white rice. Avoid traditional pickles and fermented foods.

protein.title: Kidney-Safe Protein Sources (Low PO₄ & Low K)
protein.description: High-quality protein options that are low in both phosphorus and potassium

pr1.title: Best Protein Choices for Dialysis
pr1.content: Egg whites are the gold standard - complete protein with minimal phosphorus and potassium. Fish and chicken breast are excellent secondary choices.

pr2.title: Portion Control for Protein
pr2.content: Limit protein to 1.2g/kg body weight daily. For a 60kg person, this is about 70g protein total. Track portions carefully.

pr3.title: Protein Timing with Phosphate Binders
pr3.content: Always take phosphate binders with protein-containing meals. Time binders with the first bite of dal, meat, or egg dishes.

pr4.title: Plant Protein Limitations
pr4.content: Significantly limit dal, rajma, and other legumes due to high phosphorus and potassium. If consuming, soak overnight and use small portions (1/4 cup).

fluid.title: Fluid Overload Management
fluid.description: Low-fluid content foods and hydration strategies for dialysis patients

f1.title: Hidden Fluid Sources to Avoid
f1.content: Avoid soups, dal with excess liquid, juicy fruits, ice cream, and yogurt drinks. These contribute significantly to fluid intake.

f2.title: Dry Snack Alternatives
f2.content: Choose dry snacks like plain biscuits, roasted rice (भुजा), and small amounts of dry fruits. These provide nutrition without excess fluid.

f3.title: Thirst Management Techniques
f3.content: Use ice chips, sugar-free gum, or lemon wedges to manage thirst. Rinse mouth without swallowing. Keep track of all fluid intake.

f4.title: Cooking Methods to Reduce Fluid
f4.content: Steam vegetables instead of boiling, grill or roast meats, prepare thick dal rather than watery. Drain excess liquid from cooked foods.

rice-guide.title: Smart Rice Choices for Kidney & Diabetes Patients
rice-guide.description: Condition-specific rice selection and preparation guidelines

rice1.title: CKD (Non-Dialysis) Rice Recommendations
rice1.content: Choose white rice varieties like Mota Chamal or Ukhuwa Chamal. Avoid brown, red, and black rice due to high potassium and phosphorus content. Limit portions to 150g cooked rice per meal.

rice2.title: Dialysis Patient Rice Guidelines
rice2.content: White rice varieties are safe with increased protein needs. Can consume 180-200g cooked rice per meal. Chiura (चिउरा) is excellent for fluid restriction.

rice3.title: Diabetes-Friendly Rice Choices
rice3.content: If kidney function is normal, choose Kalo Chamal (black rice) or Rato Chamal (red rice) for low glycemic index. If you have kidney disease, stick to small portions of white rice with protein and vegetables.

rice4.title: Fluid Restriction and Rice
rice4.content: Chiura (चिउरा) is perfect for patients with fluid restrictions as it requires minimal water. Soak briefly and consume. Avoid rice porridge or watery rice preparations.

rice5.title: Rice Cooking Tips for Kidney Patients
rice5.content: Wash rice thoroughly before cooking to reduce mineral content. Use appropriate water ratios. For CKD patients, cook with extra water and drain excess to reduce potassium by 10-15%.

tarkari-safety.title: Tarkari (Vegetable) Safety Guide for Kidney Patients
tarkari-safety.description: Safe vegetable choices and preparation methods for optimal kidney health

tark1.title: Low-Potassium Safe Vegetables (Daily Use)
tark1.content: Choose lauka (bottle gourd), pharsi (pumpkin), kakro (cucumber), and jhinge (ridge gourd) for daily consumption. These vegetables are naturally low in potassium and safe for both CKD and dialysis patients.

tark2.title: Medium-Potassium Vegetables: Double Boiling Required
tark2.content: Cauliflower, cabbage, green beans, and mustard greens can be consumed safely with proper preparation. Cut small, boil for 5 minutes, discard water completely, then boil again in fresh water.

tark3.title: High-Potassium Vegetables to Avoid
tark3.content: Completely avoid or severely limit spinach (palungo), potato (aloo), tomato (golbheda), and broccoli. These contain very high potassium levels that can be dangerous for kidney patients.

tark4.title: Traditional Nepali Vegetable Preparation
tark4.content: Modify traditional tarkari preparation by avoiding excess salt, using minimal oil, and incorporating double-boiling for medium potassium vegetables. Replace salt with fresh herbs like ginger, garlic, and coriander.

tark5.title: Portion Control for Vegetables
tark5.content: Safe vegetables: 1-2 cups per meal. Medium-risk vegetables (double-boiled): 1/2-3/4 cup per meal. High-risk vegetables: 1/4 cup or less, only occasionally and with special preparation.

achar-safety.title: Achar Safety: Pickle Use in CKD & Dialysis Patients
achar-safety.description: Safe pickle consumption guidelines and traditional condiment modifications for kidney patients

achar1.title: Safe Achar Choices for Daily Use
achar1.content: Choose fresh herb-based achars like coriander (धनिया) and mint (पुदिना) pickles. These are naturally low in potassium and sodium when prepared with minimal salt. Limit portions to 1-2 teaspoons per meal.

achar2.title: High-Risk Achars to Completely Avoid
achar2.content: Completely avoid tomato achar (गोलभेडा अचार), potato pickle (आलु अचार), and gundruk achar (गुन्द्रुक अचार). These contain extremely high levels of potassium and sodium that can be dangerous for kidney patients.

achar3.title: Portion Control and Preparation Methods
achar3.content: Even safe achars must be limited to very small portions. Use 1 teaspoon or less per meal. For commercial achars, rinse with water before eating to reduce sodium content.

achar4.title: Traditional Festival Food Modifications
achar4.content: During festivals and special occasions, replace traditional high-risk achars with kidney-safe alternatives. Use fresh coriander chutney, mint sauce, or homemade low-salt preparations to maintain cultural food practices safely.

achar5.title: Understanding Achar Risk Factors
achar5.content: Learn to identify high-risk ingredients: fermented vegetables increase potassium bioavailability, excess salt causes fluid retention, and high-potassium vegetables like tomatoes can cause dangerous heart rhythm problems.
